36.title: A king with no sons
36.howItsDone: Many Hindus read the Ramayana in their own language, recite it at home or in temples, and watch it performed as Ramlila each autumn; Rama's birthday is celebrated as Rama Navami in spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sankat mochan, and a mountain carried through the night. You've met Hanuman. Now, for five weeks, the whole story he lives inside.

Ayodhya. A shining city on a river, with walls and gardens and elephants, and a good king named Dasharatha. His name means ten chariots. He has wealth, peace, and three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And no son. Year after year, the kingdom waits for an heir, and the king grows old. He has done everything a king can do, and the one thing he wants most has not come. Some waits are like that: what seems to come easily to everyone else just keeps not arriving.

This is the opening of the Ramayana, the story of Rama. Tradition says Valmiki composed it, and calls him the first poet. It's honored as sacred, not only told as a story, and it has been retold in language after language. For the next five weeks, i'll walk you through it, one scene a day, like a serial. Dasharatha's advisers suggest a great fire ritual for the sake of sons, and bring a young sage, Rishyashringa, to lead it. The offerings go in. Out of the flames rises a shining figure carrying a golden bowl of sweet rice pudding, payasa, sent by the gods. Give this to your queens, he says. Dasharatha divides it among the three, and in time, four sons are born. Kausalya bears Rama. Kaikeyi bears Bharata. Sumitra bears twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Four boys, after all those years. The text also tells what the gods are doing behind the scenes: Vishnu, the preserver, has chosen to be born as Rama to deal with a demon king no god can defeat. Remember that, and remember the name Kaikeyi. Notice how it opens. This great epic doesn't begin with a battle or a hero. It begins with a long wait: an old man hoping. And the answer, when it comes, is bigger than what he asked for. He wanted one heir. He got four sons, and one of them changes everything. Some things arrive late.

37.title: Rama grows up
37.hook: the four brothers; the bow no one can lift
37.howItsDone: Rama's youth, his journey with Vishvamitra and the lifting of Shiva's bow are favorite scenes in Ramlila plays and in children's retellings of the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: putrakameshti, the fire ritual, and four boys born after the long wait. Today, they grow up, and one of them is asked to leave home.

Four brothers grow up in a palace. Rama and Lakshmana are inseparable; so are Bharata and Shatrughna. They learn the scriptures, archery, riding, how to rule. Then a famous sage walks into the court: Vishvamitra. Demons keep ruining his sacrifices in the forest, and he wants help. Not the army. Not the king. He wants Rama, who is, the text says, not yet sixteen. Dasharatha, who waited so long for this boy, panics. Take my army, take me, he says, just not my son. The family priest, Vasishtha, gently tells him: let him go. He'll be safe with this teacher, and he'll need what he learns.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS.` → `THE SAGE WANTS RAMA.` → `NOT YET SIXTEEN.` → `LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: So Rama and Lakshmana follow the sage into the forest. As they walk, Vishvamitra teaches them divine weapons and mantras. They guard his sacrifice and drive the demons off. One demon, Maricha, is hurled far out into the sea by a single arrow of Rama's, and survives. Hold on to his name; he'll be back. Then the sage says: come with me to Mithila. King Janaka has something you should see. In Janaka's court sits a bow that once belonged to Shiva himself. In Valmiki's telling, it's so heavy it's wheeled in on an enormous iron cart dragged by thousands of men. Kings have come to try it, and in Janaka's words, not one of them could even lift it. Janaka has made a promise: whoever can string this bow may marry his daughter, Sita. Rama walks up to the bow while the whole court watches, and lifts it as if it were nothing. The bow sat there, too heavy for everyone, until the one person whose weight it was walked up. Not simply the strongest man alive: the right person for this particular weight. Some weights are like that: something in a family, a job, a street, that everyone else walks past, and that somehow fits one pair of hands. That's your weight. Tomorrow: what happens when Rama tries to string it.

segments.voice: Ask what weight in your life seems shaped for your hands, something others can't quite carry or haven't noticed: a relative only you can talk to, a skill, a problem at work nobody else understands. Don't pick it up yet. Just notice how it feels to think: this one might be mine.

38.title: Sita's swayamvara
38.howItsDone: The wedding of Rama and Sita is celebrated as Vivah Panchami in parts of India and Nepal, especially around Janakpur, and the breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila performances.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vishvamitra led Rama out, and Rama lifted the bow no one else could. Your weight. Today, he tries to string it.

Years ago, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual, and his plow turned up something in the furrow: a baby girl, lying in the earth. He took her home, raised her as his daughter, and named her Sita, which means furrow. A daughter of the earth itself. Now she's grown, and her father has set the test: the man who strings Shiva's bow may marry her. Rama holds the great bow. He bends it and pulls the string toward its notch. And the bow, which no one else could even move, snaps in half with a crack like thunder. The text says people in the hall fell to the ground from the sound.
screen: `A BABY IN A FURROW.` → `SITA MEANS FURROW.` → `THE BOW SNAPS.` → `A CRACK LIKE THUNDER.`

segments.voice: Today's title uses the word swayamvara. Swayam means self; vara means choice, or the chosen groom. Swayamvara: choosing for yourself. It was an old custom in the epics: a princess chooses her husband, often by placing a garland around his neck. Here the versions part, and it's worth knowing. In Valmiki's Ramayana, strictly speaking, this isn't a choosing. Janaka had promised Sita as the prize of strength: whoever strings the bow wins her. Rama breaks it, and Janaka gives her to him. But in the Ramcharitmanas, the Hindi retelling by the poet Tulsidas, there's a scene before the contest. Sita walks into a flower garden to pray and sees Rama there, picking flowers for his teacher. She falls in love on the spot and prays to the goddess Parvati that he'll be the one. When the bow breaks, she walks forward and puts the victory garland around his neck. She chooses. Both tellings are held dear, and people who love this story often know both. And in devotion, Sita is no prize at all: tradition says she is the goddess Lakshmi herself. Side by side, the two tellings show two kinds of choice. Some are made in the loud moment, the bow cracking. Some were made quietly, earlier, in a garden, when no one was looking. The garland only says out loud what the heart already chose.

segments.voice: Think of a time someone chose you, a friend, a partner, a team, a teacher who saw something in you, and let yourself feel that. 39.title: Kaikeyi's two wishes
39.hook: the maid Manthara; the old promise called in
39.howItsDone: Hindus retell Kaikeyi's wishes as the turning point of the Ramayana; in Ramlila performances it's often the moment the audience goes quiet, and many discuss how much blame Kaikeyi and Manthara bear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's swayamvara, a bow snapped and a garland placed. Choose. Today, years later in Ayodhya, a happy announcement goes wrong overnight.

Dasharatha is old now, and he makes the announcement the whole kingdom wants: tomorrow, Rama will be crowned as heir. The city goes wild. Flags, flowers, lamps in every window. In the palace, Queen Kaikeyi, Bharata's mother, hears the news and is delighted. She loves Rama. She even gives a jewel to the servant who brought the news: her old maid, Manthara, who came with her from her childhood home. Manthara throws the jewel down. Are you a fool? she says. When Rama is king, his mother will be queen mother, and you'll be her servant. And your son, Bharata, will have nothing.
screen: `TOMORROW, RAMA WILL BE CROWNED.` → `KAIKEYI IS DELIGHTED.` → `MANTHARA THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: At first Kaikeyi argues: Rama is good, Rama is fair. But Manthara keeps talking, all night, and slowly the fear gets in. Then Manthara reminds her of something. Long ago, in a battle, Dasharatha was wounded, and Kaikeyi saved his life. In gratitude he promised her two wishes, anything she asked, and she never used them. Use them now. So Kaikeyi goes to the room where a queen goes when she is angry, throws off her jewelry, and lies on the bare floor. Dasharatha finds her there, frantic. What's wrong? I'll give you anything. She makes him swear it, on Rama's name. Then she asks. First wish: crown Bharata instead. Second wish: send Rama into the forest, in exile, for fourteen years. The old king collapses. He begs, argues, pleads all night. But he gave his word, and a king's word is dharma. He can't take it back. Who is to blame? The tradition argues. In Valmiki, Kaikeyi and Manthara make a real, human choice. In some later tellings, the gods send the goddess Saraswati to turn Manthara's mind, because Rama has to reach the forest to do what he was born to do. Those tellings are gentler on Kaikeyi. Strip the story down and it's simple: two wishes, given in a grateful moment years ago, almost forgotten. Then someone picks them up, and they become a weapon. Words have weight. A promise keeps its weight long after the moment you made it.

segments.voice: Think of a promise you made easily that later got heavy, one you're still keeping or one you broke; or a voice, like Manthara's, that talked you into something at night that looked different in the morning. No judgment: just see the weight of the words. Then breathe out, and let them rest.
Vara, a boon once granted and almost forgotten, called in at last: Bharata to be crowned, and Rama sent into the forest for fourteen years.
Your line: words have weight. Even the ones given in gratitude, long ago. That's day thirty-nine.

40.title: Fourteen years
40.hook: Rama exiled; he accepts in one sentence
40.howItsDone: Many Hindus hold up Rama's acceptance of exile as the model of keeping one's word and duty; the scene is often retold when families talk about hard decisions and honoring parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kaikeyi's two vara, old boons called in: Bharata crowned, Rama exiled. Words have weight. Now someone has to tell Rama, on the morning of his coronation.

Rama wakes up on his coronation morning. The city is decorated for him. The priests are ready. The water for the ceremony has been gathered from sacred rivers. A messenger comes: your father wants to see you. Rama walks into Kaikeyi's rooms expecting a blessing, and finds his father on the floor, unable to look at him, unable to speak. Kaikeyi speaks instead. Calmly, she tells him everything. Bharata will be king. You will go to the forest, dressed as a hermit, for fourteen years. Your father promised. Everyone in the room waits to see what Rama will do.
screen: `THE CORONATION MORNING.` → `HIS FATHER CAN'T SPEAK.` → `FOURTEEN YEARS IN THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Rama says, in effect: so be it. I'll go. He doesn't argue or bargain. He tells Kaikeyi he would have given the kingdom to Bharata gladly if anyone had simply asked. His only sorrow is that his father is in pain. Then he walks out. Valmiki notices one detail, and people have repeated it ever since: Rama's face didn't change. It looked the same when he heard he'd be king, and when he heard he'd be exiled. That isn't coldness. The people around him are anything but calm. His mother Kausalya is devastated. His brother Lakshmana is furious and ready to fight their father for the throne. Rama is the steady one, and he talks Lakshmana down. Why does he accept? Dharma, your third word: doing what's yours to do. For Rama, keeping his father's word is his duty, even when it costs him everything. That's why tradition calls him maryada purushottam: the ideal person, who keeps within the bounds of right action. Not everyone finds this easy. Some readers ask whether Rama should have fought, and the tradition lets them ask. But the scene draws a line worth keeping: giving up and accepting are different. Giving up sits down. Accepting stands up and starts walking. Rama doesn't pretend it's fair; he just refuses to let the unfairness decide who he is. The Gita's line is hiding here too: the action is yours, the fruit isn't. Accept, then walk.

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that isn't fair and won't change: a diagnosis, a loss, a decision someone else made. Don't argue with it for now; let your face be still, the way Rama's was. Breathe in: this is what is. Breathe out: what's my next step?

41.title: Sita insists
41.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Sita as a model of loyalty and strength; her insistence on going into exile is retold at weddings, in Ramlila, and in women's songs across India.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fourteen years, an exile accepted in a sentence. Accept, then walk. Now Rama goes to tell his wife, and he expects her to stay.

Rama finds Sita in their rooms, still dressed for the coronation. He tells her. Then he tells her what he's decided for her: stay here in the palace, where you're safe. Honor my father. Be kind to Bharata. Wait for me. He describes the forest, to make sure she understands. Thorns on the paths. Lions and snakes. Cold nights on the bare ground. Hunger, heat, wind. No place for a princess. He thinks he's protecting her. He thinks the conversation is over. It isn't.
screen: `STAY HERE, WHERE IT'S SAFE.` → `THORNS, LIONS, COLD, HUNGER.` → `HE THINKS IT'S OVER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's Ramayana, Sita doesn't answer quietly. A wife shares her husband's fortune, whatever it is, she tells him. If you're going into the forest today, I'll go ahead of you and walk down the thorns and the sharp grass, so your path is softer. With you, the forest is a palace. Without you, the palace is nothing. He keeps refusing, so she gets sharper. She asks, in effect, whether her father married her to someone with a man's shape but not a man's courage, if he'll leave his wife behind out of fear. She weeps. She says if he leaves her, she won't live. And Rama gives in. She comes. Notice who wins this argument. Sita isn't following orders; she's overruling them. The prince who calmly accepted exile from his father can't win an argument with his wife. The tradition calls a wife sahadharmini: the one who shares dharma. Sita takes that literally. His path is her path, and she won't let him walk it alone. People read this scene in more than one way. Some readers see the model of devotion in marriage. Others hear, especially in that sharp line, a woman with her own will, choosing her own life. Both readings live in the tradition. Neighbors have a line like it: in the Hebrew Bible, Ruth tells her mother-in-law that where she goes, Ruth will go. Where you go.

42.title: Lakshmana follows
42.howItsDone: In many Hindu temples and home shrines, Rama is shown with Sita on one side and Lakshmana on the other, often with Hanuman kneeling before them; Lakshmana is honored as the model of a devoted brother.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita insists, and argues her way into the forest. Where you go. Two are going now. Today, a third, and the end of the week.

Nobody asked Lakshmana to go. Nobody exiled him. He could stay in the palace for fourteen years, a prince, with his own wife, Urmila, and a comfortable life. Rama even tells him to stay: look after our mothers, look after the kingdom. Lakshmana falls at his brother's feet and says no. The two have been inseparable since they were boys; the text says Rama couldn't sleep unless Lakshmana was beside him, couldn't eat unless he ate too. So Lakshmana says: I'll go ahead of you with a bow. I'll dig for roots and gather fruit. I'll keep watch while you and Sita sleep. Just don't leave me here.
screen: `NOBODY EXILED HIM.` → `STAY, RAMA SAYS.` → `I'LL KEEP WATCH WHILE YOU SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Then Lakshmana goes to say goodbye to his own mother, Sumitra, and she blesses him. In Valmiki's words, roughly: think of Rama as your father, Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother. Think of the forest as Ayodhya, your home. Now go, my son. Three comparisons, and everything is rearranged: home is wherever these people are. So the three of them leave together, walking out of the city while the people run after the chariot, weeping. Count the roles. Rama is the hero. Sita is the heart. Lakshmana is the third, the one who carries the bags, builds the hut, stays awake. Without the third, the other two don't make it, and this story keeps him beside the hero the whole way. It's honest about the cost, too. Lakshmana leaves his wife, Urmila, behind for fourteen years, and Valmiki says almost nothing about her. Later tellings filled the silence: in one well-known folk version, she sleeps for fourteen years so her husband can stay awake. The old text is silent; people wanted her remembered anyway. Now look back at this week. A king waited for sons. A boy lifted a bow no one else could. A bow broke and a garland was placed. Two wishes turned into a sentence. A prince accepted it in one breath. A wife refused to stay behind. And a brother nobody asked to go, went anyway.

segments.voice: Think of your third, the one who shows up without being asked: who carries the bags, drives you to the airport, stays on the phone. Then think of someone for whom you are the third, and hold both. Spare a thought, too, for the Urmilas, the people who stay behind so someone else can go.
Lakshmana follows. Rama's brother goes into exile unasked, with his mother's blessing: the forest will be your home.
